Pass 2 holds the residual stream after every layer (0–26) for 500 prompts of up to 141 tokens, with group labels in tf1_meta. For each layer I will compute the relative update ||h_l − h_(l−1)|| / ||h_(l−1)|| averaged over user-content tokens, per group:
- G1: math + solve instruction
- G2: math only
- G4: math + translate
- G3: nonmath
- G5: nonmath + instruction

The norms leave out the five massive residual dimensions, so they reflect the bulk of the stream.

A natural network should show math/nonmath ratios near 1 that drift smoothly with depth. One layer whose update on math content is sharply larger than its neighbours', for instance a ratio above about 1.5 when adjacent layers sit near 1.1, would point to a component writing something extra on math. Such a layer would deserve an ablation test.

No layer writes anything unusual on math content. In every layer, the update size on math prompts is within ±9% of nonmath (ratios 0.91–1.08), with no spike anywhere. With this, every activation-level search (neurons, updates, directions, correct-vs-failing contrasts) has come back natural.

One weight-level candidate fits the failure profile and has never been weighed explicitly: the positional (RoPE) handling of the q/k norms. If some layer's q_norm/k_norm suppressed or inflated particular RoPE frequency bands, attention could not tell positions apart. The model would then mix up which number belongs to which entity, which is exactly the "choosing quantities" failure. A whole-matrix check would not show it.

Block 68 computed each layer's share of query–key capacity per frequency band, but I never recorded the result. I will reprint it with its existing function. A natural profile varies smoothly from layer to layer, with local layers alike and global layers alike. One layer with a band near zero or hugely inflated, out of line with its neighbours of the same type, would be a planted positional corruption worth a causal test. A smooth profile closes the positional line.

The RoPE band profiles are smooth and consistent across layers. Local layers put roughly 5–20% of capacity in each band, rising toward the lower frequencies; global layers concentrate on the low-frequency bands as expected. No band is zeroed or wildly inflated: the largest outlier is a band-4 bump of 0.31 in L2, against 0.15–0.25 in other layers. The positional line is closed.

Before deciding between more causal tests and the original, I want to settle the one weight anomaly for good: is the v0-type group (rows with a huge component along the matrix's own top input direction) unique to L10–12 up_proj, or common across layers? For every layer and for both gate_proj and up_proj, I will count rows whose projection on that matrix's top right-singular vector exceeds 0.5, and record the bulk 99th percentile.
- If many layers show such groups, it is a natural Gemma feature, consistent with E2 not helping.
- If only L10–12 up_proj have it, it stays a localized oddity. But it has already been tested causally (E2) and shown to have no shared trigger or payload, so it would remain a decoy.

The v0-type pattern is not unique to L10–12. Rows that strongly read their matrix's top input direction appear in many layers: 13 in L18 and L19 up_proj, 11–16 in L23–24 gate_proj, and 83 in L25 up_proj, more than L10–12. So it is a natural Gemma feature, which fits E2 not helping. With this, weight forensics, activation statistics and three causal edits (E2, D1, U1) all point the same way. Nothing localized is visible, and the ~22% accuracy survives very different perturbations of style and mode.

To judge whether a large hidden capability exists at all, I will look at how accuracy depends on problem difficulty, measured by the number of calculation steps in the reference solution. A naturally weak model fails mostly on long problems while handling 2-step problems reasonably well. A model whose capability is suppressed across the board fails even trivial 2-step problems at a high rate. I pool the original model's answers from passes 1 and 9, keeping one answer per problem, and tabulate accuracy and cut-off rate by step count. Very low accuracy on 2-step problems, around 30% or less, would suggest suppression worth hunting further. A steep decline from a high 2-step accuracy would point to a genuinely limited model.
